series.title: Reading A Tale of Two Cities
series.deck: Four essays on inherited names, testimony, vengeance, and the person a category cannot see.

articles.title: He Threw Down a Coin
articles.deck: A dead child, a gold coin, and the power to declare an account closed.
body: The carriage races through a narrow Paris street. People scatter. Under its wheels a child is killed. The Marquis de Saint Evrémonde looks out, annoyed by the interruption, and asks whether his horses have been hurt. Then he reproaches the people for failing to look after their children. The street, as he understands it, exists for his carriage; anyone who cannot get out of its way has caused the difficulty.

He throws down a gold coin. He does not seem to think he is doing something especially cruel. From his side of the carriage door, he has suffered inconvenience and nevertheless offered compensation. The coin closes the account. That is what makes this scene more disturbing than a display of temper: he believes he has settled a matter that the father on the ground cannot even begin to settle.
## Who sets the price?

A child's life becomes a sum of money because one party possesses the authority to decide what the loss is worth. The father has not agreed to sell anything. The coin is not a negotiation. It is an instruction about the kind of loss he is allowed to have, and the point at which he must stop making a noise about it.

The horses belong to the Marquis. The child does not. Ownership makes the horses immediately legible as something that matters; the crying father appears as a nuisance. It is not that the Marquis has carefully weighed two equal lives and reached the wrong conclusion. He has already placed these people outside the circle in which such weighing would be necessary. His money arrives after that classification, not instead of it.

Later, talking to his nephew, he presents oppression as the reliable foundation of rule. Keep people frightened and subordinate, and the order will endure. There is no revelation waiting for him about how his estate works. He knows. What he cannot imagine is that those who bear it might acquire the power to bring it to an end.
## What the family has already done

Long before the child dies in the street, the Evrémonde brothers destroy another household. A young peasant woman attracts a nobleman's desire. Her husband is yoked to a cart like an animal, kept out at night, and worked to death; then she is taken away. Her young brother tries to defend her and is mortally wounded by a nobleman's sword. Their father dies after hearing what has happened. The woman herself dies. A younger sister, hidden away, survives.

Doctor Manette is summoned to treat the dying woman and her brother. He sees enough to understand the crime and writes to the authorities. His letter reaches the very men against whom he is appealing. They have him seized and confined in the Bastille. There is no ordinary trial at which the truth can become a defense. The mechanism meant to receive his complaint delivers him into the power he has complained about.

Eighteen years later, the doctor emerges as a man who makes shoes and answers with his prison designation: One Hundred and Five, North Tower. It is not enough to say that two men behaved abominably. Their world lets them turn the witness into the prisoner. The violence and the suppression of its record belong to the same arrangement.

The Marquis's coin is a small, visible version of that arrangement. The powerful decide what the injury is called, what it costs, and whether the injured may continue speaking. Individual brutality matters, but the order does not have to invent itself anew each time someone is brutal.
## The same afternoon

The novel's opening contrast between the best and worst of times need not describe two successive periods. Different people can inhabit opposite versions of the same afternoon. For the Marquis, this is an obstructed journey. For a father, the world has ended. They stand on the same street without being admitted to the same reality.
Someone throws the coin back into the carriage. This the Marquis finds intolerable. The child can be priced; the refusal of his price becomes an outrage. He threatens the crowd and drives on.

The child's father, Gaspard, clings beneath the carriage. On the night of his return to the château, the Marquis is murdered. A note invokes the name Jacques. Gaspard is eventually caught and hanged on a conspicuously high gallows, his body made into a public warning. The power that could not hear a father's grief knows how to display his punishment. The returned coin and the murder do not restore the child; they show an account that was never closed.
## A nephew who leaves

The Marquis's nephew refuses the inheritance: the title, the estate, the income, the family name. He leaves for England, earns his living teaching French, and calls himself Charles Darnay. He marries Doctor Manette's daughter. Where his uncle sees a permanent order, he recognizes something from which he must separate himself.

But a name can be relinquished by its bearer and retained by everyone who judges him. Years later, Darnay will discover that the revolution does not necessarily read his life as he has lived it. The nephew who refuses to belong to the Evrémondes will be condemned for belonging to them. That is the next essay's question: what does a refusal mean when it cannot make others stop classifying you?

articles.title: He Renounced Everything—and It Did Not Help
articles.deck: Darnay refuses the inheritance, but cannot make others relinquish his name.
body: Charles Darnay was born an Evrémonde. The name would have given him a château, an estate, an income and the right to live on the labor of people he had never needed to meet. He does not merely announce that he dislikes the abuses attached to it. He refuses the position from which he would continue to benefit.

On the night that ends in his uncle's murder, the two men confront one another. The uncle regards domination as the foundation of the family. The nephew sees a history of injury and a debt that he cannot discharge by inheriting more comfortably. To the Marquis, earning one's living is a descent into absurdity. To Darnay, it is the beginning of a life he might answer for.
## The departure is real

He gives up the estate's income and makes humane arrangements through Gabelle, the steward. In England he teaches and translates French. He uses Darnay rather than Evrémonde and builds an ordinary household with Lucie Manette. On the morning of their wedding he tells her father his true identity, as he had promised. The name is not concealed from the one person whose knowledge most matters to that marriage.

This is more than changing the sign on an unchanged fortune. The relinquishment costs him the ease and authority his birth offered. He cannot erase the past, but he can refuse to make its advantages the basis of his own future. That distinction will matter even when the refusal fails to protect him.

Gabelle later writes from prison. He has been accused of serving an emigrant nobleman, although he carried out Darnay's instructions to reduce the burdens placed on the tenants. His plea places a concrete responsibility before Darnay: a man who acted for him is now in danger because of that connection.

Darnay returns to France to save him. He believes that his renunciation and his conduct can be explained, that revolutionary justice will distinguish him from the men he repudiated. Leaving letters for Lucie and Doctor Manette, he travels toward a country whose rules are changing faster than his understanding of them.
## The name comes back

He is arrested as an emigrant aristocrat and imprisoned for more than a year. At his first trial, Doctor Manette's standing as a survivor of the Bastille helps secure his release. The crowd celebrates the acquitted prisoner and carries him home. That evening he is arrested again.

At the second trial the Defarges produce a manuscript found in the doctor's former cell when the Bastille fell. It recounts the destruction of the peasant family and the doctor's own disappearance into prison. At its end, the imprisoned Manette denounces the Evrémonde brothers and their descendants. Words written in captivity, without knowledge of the future household, now become evidence against his daughter's husband.

Darnay is sentenced to death within twenty-four hours. The decisive story is not a story of something he has done. It is the story of a family from which he tried to withdraw. His father-in-law, who has spent his regained strength saving him, is made to appear as his accuser.

A person may surrender property and refuse a name. He cannot alone compel other people to change the category under which they file him. The classification belongs, in this moment, to those who pronounce the sentence. What Darnay chose becomes secondary to what they say he is.
## A testimony taken from its speaker

This does not make the old order and the revolution interchangeable. Their histories, their duration and the injuries that produce them are different. To notice a repeated mechanism is not to cancel those differences. The child under the carriage was not responsible for obstructing aristocratic life; Darnay is not personally responsible for his father's crimes. In each case, the category does work that attention to the person would interrupt.

Nor should Manette's manuscript be treated as proof that a victim ought to have remained silent. His testimony is necessary. Those deaths and his eighteen stolen years deserve a record. The terrible turn is that the record is detached from the living man who wrote it. A curse born in imprisonment becomes an instrument he is no longer allowed to interpret, qualify or withdraw.

The doctor knows Darnay now. He knows his daughter and granddaughter. None of that present knowledge can reach the words being read in court. After the sentence, he breaks down and returns to shoemaking. The former prison has recovered him through the very document in which he tried to preserve his voice.
## A choice is not an insurance policy

It would be too easy to conclude that Darnay's renunciation was pointless because it did not save him. That measures a moral act solely by the protection it purchases. His instructions mattered to the people living on the estate. His refusal also determined what he was willing to do with his own life. Neither fact disappears when a tribunal refuses to recognize it.

He did not leave because his uncle approved, because gratitude was assured, or because history had promised him a safe passage. He left because continuing to occupy that position was intolerable to him. His choice cannot command the world's recognition. It remains a choice he made.

The next essay turns to someone who has overwhelming reasons not to recognize a distinction between one Evrémonde and another. Madame Defarge is not a spectator who has acquired a fashionable taste for vengeance. She is the surviving younger sister of the household the brothers destroyed. Her reasons must be heard before we ask what she does with them.

articles.title: She Had Every Reason
articles.deck: Her loss is real. Does it give her a claim upon another child?
body: Madame Defarge sits knitting in the wine-shop. People pass, conversations unfold, names are noticed. The quiet work is also a register of people marked for death. To her, what has been entered there seems as fixed as the stars. The patient surface of the scene contains years in which patience has meant waiting for the power to act.

She is the younger sister who escaped when the Evrémonde brothers destroyed her family. Her sister was taken, her sister's husband worked to death, her brother fatally wounded, her father broken by the news. Her sister died too. The child who survived grew up, married, and came to sit behind this counter with her knitting. Before confronting the nobleman, her brother took his younger sister beyond their reach.
## Begin with everything done to her

There is no honest reading in which this injury is a misunderstanding. Nor was there a functioning court that she simply neglected to approach. The doctor who reported the crime disappeared into the Bastille for eighteen years. The authority to which a victim might appeal belonged to the same world as the perpetrators.

When revolution arrives, she has reasons to believe that only the destruction of that world can end its impunity. At the fall of the Bastille she is no longer waiting silently. Later, beside the guillotine, the knitting continues. Her register has acquired an apparatus capable of carrying out its sentences.

The brothers themselves are already dead by the revolutionary trials. But for her the family is not finished. Darnay's repudiation of it does not settle the debt. Neither does the sentence that will take his life. She wants Lucie and the child as well.

Her husband hesitates. He is a revolutionary too; he has lived among the same suffering and helped bring the manuscript into court. Yet he thinks Doctor Manette has suffered enough, and he would spare the wife and daughter. Madame Defarge rejects the proposed stopping point. One might as well ask the wind or fire to stop, she suggests.
## When a child becomes a root

The reasoning is not without a structure. The family's wealth and security grew from violence. Its descendants carry a future from which the destroyed peasant family was excluded. Leave a branch alive and the old power may grow again. To eliminate the wrong completely, she believes she must eliminate the line.

But Lucie's little daughter is not a branch. She is a child. To make her death seem necessary, one must look through her and see a hereditary category in her place. The Marquis did something comparable when he saw an obstruction instead of the child his carriage had killed. The injuries and positions are radically unequal; the act of replacing a person with a classification can nevertheless recur.

Calling Madame Defarge a monster would spare us the difficult part of Dickens's construction. He first gives her loss its full weight. Then he shows her preparing to kill another child. We cannot honestly deny the first fact in order to condemn the second, or use the first to make the second disappear.

Nor is this an instruction that victims should simply forgive and move on. The question is not whether her anger is sufficiently polite. It is whether another person's existence can be cancelled by a debt that person did not incur. The old order has taught a language of inherited status and expendable lives. Its victim can use that language against it without ceasing to endanger those who never wielded its power.
## The woman at the door

Madame Defarge goes to Lucie's lodging, intending to find evidence and advance the prosecution of the family. Lucie and the others have already left. Miss Pross remains. The two women have no shared language adequate to the argument, but each understands the other's purpose well enough.

Miss Pross does not answer the history of the Evrémondes. She does not offer a theory of revolution or ask that the wronged family accept its loss. She stands between the intruder and the people she loves. They struggle. Madame Defarge's pistol goes off and kills its owner; the blast leaves Miss Pross deaf.

This is not a court reaching a judgment on historical suffering. It is a woman refusing to let another woman pass through a particular door. The protected people have names and faces for her. That limited, concrete allegiance is precisely what the comprehensive argument about exterminating a line cannot admit.
## Not an inevitable inheritance

Dickens's revolutionary scenes can be criticized for their horror of crowds: the grindstone, the dancing, the knitting, the machinery of death. His fear of collective violence is unmistakable. Yet it would be inaccurate to say he makes the old regime innocent so that the revolution can appear wicked. The novel takes pains to show what produced the rage.

The harder reading holds both things together. The old order's crime includes the habits of perception it leaves behind. Still, those habits are not a fate that every injured person must obey. Defarge's hesitation matters. He shares the cause and knows the history, but reaches a point at which he says enough. His wife's continuation is a decision, not the automatic movement of an impersonal wind.

Meanwhile Darnay's execution appears unavoidable. The law will not distinguish the heir who refused his inheritance from the family that committed the crimes. An English lawyer, Sydney Carton, has promised Lucie that he would give his life for her or someone she loves. He looks extraordinarily like her husband. In the final essay, that resemblance will expose another limit of the classification: the guillotine cannot tell the two men apart.

articles.title: The Guillotine Cannot Tell Them Apart
articles.deck: The substitute, the withheld consent, and the seamstress who sees the difference.
body: Long before the Paris prison, there is a London courtroom. Darnay is accused of treason. A witness is confident of his identification. Sydney Carton, who has seemed more interested in the ceiling than in the proceedings, passes a note to the lawyer Stryver. He draws attention to the resemblance between himself and the accused. If two men can look so alike, how certain can the witness be? The identification weakens, and Darnay escapes conviction.
The first rescue uses resemblance to open a doubt. The last will use it to satisfy a certainty: the authorities believe they know which man must die and need only a body to place beneath that name.
## A promise without a claim

Carton supplies much of the intelligence behind Stryver's successful legal work. He is capable, drinks heavily, and understands his life as a disappointment. That is not the same as having no relationships or no possible future. It is the judgment from within which he has difficulty imagining either.

He visits Lucie and tells her what her presence has awakened in him: a sense of the life he might have lived. He does not make her responsible for bringing it into being. He does not demand that she love him instead of Darnay or offer his unhappiness as a debt she owes. He promises that he would give his life for her or for anyone dear to her. Then he leaves. The promise is not followed by years of claims upon her gratitude.

In Paris, after Darnay's death sentence, Carton identifies Barsad, the spy who is also Miss Pross's brother. He uses his knowledge of Barsad's compromising identity and spying to force cooperation. He secures access to the prison and obtains substances from a chemist. The novel does not need to name them for us to understand the plan.
## The man being saved does not agree

In the cell, Carton tells Darnay to exchange clothes with him. Darnay resists the apparent impossibility of what he is proposing. Carton dictates a letter, brings the drug to his face, and renders him unconscious. The exchange is completed. Barsad has the insensible Darnay carried out as Carton, while Carton remains to die as Darnay. The rescued man is taken toward safety before he can choose otherwise.

That is not a minor detail to be dissolved in admiration. Carton acts without Darnay's consent. A person may reasonably refuse to live at another's expense, and Carton prevents him from exercising that refusal. The rescue contains coercion even though its purpose is loving.

There is also a distinction between this act and assigning someone else to die for a cause. Carton takes the condemned place himself. He does not nominate a third person as expendable. Yet it would be false to say that nobody else bears a cost or takes a risk: the helpers participate, and the people who love or remember him will live with the loss. The moral difficulty should remain visible rather than be bought off with an arithmetic of lives.
## The right name on the wrong body

Darnay was condemned because of the category Evrémonde. The prison now accepts a substitute because it does not recognize the person beneath the clothing and name. Physical resemblance is indispensable to the plot. But the plot also makes visible a system whose confidence in a classification exceeds its interest in knowing the individual it kills.

Carton does not answer that system with an opposing category. He is not saving a representative aristocrat in the name of aristocracy. He is saving Lucie's husband and her daughter's father. His reason is particular. That does not automatically justify every means he uses; it explains why the tribunal's judgment fails to settle the matter for him.

As the prisoners are gathered before execution, a young seamstress recognizes that he is not Darnay. The resemblance that deceives the machinery does not deceive someone who has attended to the man. She understands enough of the exchange to keep his secret. She says she is not afraid, but is small and weak; she asks to hold his hand for greater courage. The novel gives no assurance that exposing him would save her; keeping the secret is not a bargain whose alternative reward we can calculate.

They hold hands on the journey and until the final separation, when they kiss and bless one another. She does not need his family history in order to recognize his kindness. He cannot save her from the sentence, but he can remain with her in her final moments. Amid the processing of condemned bodies, two people still see each other. It is a smaller act than the substitution, and no less essential to the ending's meaning.
## Who calls a life better?

The novel closes with a vision of a future in which Carton is remembered, including a child who bears his name. These are not recorded last words spoken on the scaffold. The narrator imagines what his thoughts might have expressed if they had been uttered and were prophetic. The famous judgment about a better deed and a better rest belongs within that conditional frame.

To read it as proof that an unsuccessful man's life becomes valuable only when he dies usefully would repeat the pricing we began by resisting. No spectator has the right to decide that Carton's years are worth less than Darnay's, or that another disappointed person ought to seek the same ending. The imagined consolation is not a general rule prescribing sacrifice.

Across these essays, the Marquis prices a child; Darnay refuses an inheritance without gaining control of his classification; Manette loses authority over his own testimony; Madame Defarge turns a real debt into a claim against another child. None of these movements is undone by one man's death. The guillotine continues its work.

But its inability to distinguish two men is not the novel's only account of what people can see. There is also the seamstress, who notices the difference, and the hand she asks to hold. Against the category that knows everything in advance, there remains the encounter in which someone looks again.
